[top model]: The Model That Builds F*cking Anything (Full Guide)

NO1ennn (@n01ennn) · Source sur X

An empty folder. 1,000+ subagents. 8 days. A working operating system that boots on a laptop.

That's what [top model] built before it was even released.

One paragraph of text turned into three working electronic devices. A black-hole calculation that nobody had finished since 2003 got finished. Fermat's Last Theorem got fully formalized by a team of 1,000 agents in 30 hours, while [advanced model] with the exact same setup got stuck at 26%.

I spent two days going through everything: the launch post, the system card, the engineering blogs, the docs, the independent leaderboards and hundreds of posts from people who got their hands on it. This is everything I found, explained in plain words, with my honest opinion on where it's worth the money and where it isn't.

My take, up front: [top model] is not a smarter chatbot. It's the first model where the limit is mostly the size of the job you're brave enough to give it. But it's also the easiest model to waste money on. Both of those things are true, and this guide covers both.

PART 1 · THE MODEL

01 · What [top model] actually is

On November 9 Anthropic shipped two names at once: [top model] and Claude Mythos 5.2. Here's the first thing people get wrong: these are not two models. It's the same model under two names.

The difference is the safeguards. [top model] has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards, so Anthropic can give it to everyone on a paid plan. Mythos is the same model without most of those safeguards, and only organizations that pass Anthropic's cyber or life-sciences verification programs can use it.

So when you use [top model], you're using the full engine. You're just not allowed to point it at exploit development or wet-lab biology.

The basics:

→ model ID: [top model] → $8 per million input tokens, $40 per million output → 1M token context window, up to 128K tokens of output → available on every paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, Enterprise), the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud and Microsoft Foundry → knowledge cutoff: June 2026

My take: the two-name setup is smart. It lets Anthropic ship the full capability to normal users without arguing about cyber and bio risk every release. For 99% of what you'd actually build, [top model] is the whole model.

02 · What changed since [previous top model]

If you used [previous top model], four things are different:

→ it's faster. Anthropic says outputs come up to 30% faster than [previous top model] → it's cheaper. $8 / $40 per million tokens, down from $10 / $50. That's 20% off → it talks more clearly. Testers found it explains itself better than past [top model] models, and this matters more than it sounds when an agent hands you a report after 6 hours of work → it refuses less by mistake. In early testing across the Claude apps, Claude Code and Cowork, Anthropic saw about 55% fewer unnecessary blocks than with [previous top model]

There's also an optional fast mode: up to 2.5x faster token generation, for $16 / $80 per million tokens. Useful when you're waiting on it live. A waste when it runs overnight.

a step above [advanced model]", clearer, up to 30% faster: the capability table post

03 · The benchmarks, read honestly

Here's the official table, turned into something you can read in 10 seconds:

What each one actually measures, in plain words:

→ Remote Labor Index: real paid remote jobs, done end to end. [top model] scores 41.3%. [advanced model] scores 21.3%. [previous top model] scored 17.9%. It more than doubled its own previous version → FrontierCode 2.0: would the maintainers of a real open-source project merge this code? 49.1% at xhigh effort, the best of any released model Anthropic tested → FrontierSWE v2: long agentic coding tasks. 69.9% vs 62.3% for [advanced model] → Terminal-Bench-Science: doing actual science work in a terminal. 74.6% vs 58.7% → OSWorld 2.1: using a computer like a person, clicking and typing. 89.3% → RoboDojo: controlling a simulated two-arm robot from camera images. 64.9%, more than double the next frontier model → Humanity's Last Exam: expert-level questions across every field, with tools. 74.2% → Chartography: reading charts and figures. 73.4%

Now the part most posts leave out. [top model] doesn't win everything:

→ on AutomationBench (business workflows), Gemini 4 Carbon scores 53.9% vs [top model]'s 51.4% → on the knowledge-work Elo in AA-Briefcase, [advanced model] sits slightly ahead (1800 vs 1785), even though [top model] wins on the rubric score

My take: look at where the biggest jumps are. Remote jobs: 2x. Robot control: 2.3x over [previous top model]. Science in a terminal: +16 points over [advanced model]. These aren't "answer the question" tests. They're "go do the thing" tests. That's the real story of this model: the gap shows up when the task is long, messy and physical, not when it's a quiz.

FrontierCode and effort: at high it matches [advanced model] at max for roughly half the cost

04 · What people outside Anthropic measured

Benchmarks from the company that sells the model are a starting point, not proof. So here's what independent testers and partners found in the first two days:

→ Artificial Analysis put it at #1 of 74 models on their Intelligence Index, with a score of 65. Gemini 4 Carbon is at 60, [advanced model] at 59 → even at high effort (not max) it scored 62, ahead of everything else, with about 40% fewer output tokens than some rivals at their top setting → on their 3D benchmark, building interactive 3D scenes, it took first place at 1271 Elo, 67 points ahead of the next model → Cursor: 60% on CursorBench at max effort, the top model they've tested. 56.9% at default effort, up from 49.2% for [previous top model] → Shortcut (financial modeling): 91% at high effort vs 86% for [previous top model]. Even at low effort it beat every other model's best score → Zapier: 2.3x better than [previous top model] on their workflows

And one honest counterexample from Artificial Analysis: on one presentation task, Gemini 4 Carbon finished in about an hour for around $8. [top model] at max took about three hours and around $68. [top model]'s deck scored higher (87% vs 72%). Better result, eight times the price. Keep that trade in mind for the rest of this guide.

PART 2 · WHAT IT BUILT

05 · An operating system from an empty folder

This is the example that made me take the model seriously.

One Anthropic engineer gave [top model] a single task: design a prototype operating system. It started from an empty folder. The model coordinated over 1,000 subagents that worked around the clock for 8 days, writing, testing and reviewing code.

The result boots on a real laptop. It has its own core that runs the machine, drivers for the disk, keyboard and network, permanent file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer, and Claude built in.

It's a prototype, not something you'd install on your work machine. But think about what had to go right for it to boot at all. Thousands of pieces written by different agents, all fitting together, tested against each other, for 8 days, without a human gluing them.

Two more coding results from the same launch:

→ a team of agents on an earlier version of [top model] moved a critical production service from Python to Rust. It now starts about 26x faster → Anthropic says over 90% of the changes merged into its own core codebase are now written by Claude, with human guidance

My take: the impressive part isn't the code. Every good model writes code now. It's the coordination. Keeping 1,000 agents pointed at one goal for 8 days is a management problem, and [top model] is solving it.

06 · Three devices from one paragraph

This one is my favorite, because it's physical. You can hold the result in your hand.

Anthropic and Diode, a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards, gave [top model] a short prompt for each of three devices: a USB speakerphone, a home voice-assistant hub and a handheld virtual pet. The speakerphone prompt was basically one sentence: a puck that plugs in over USB-C, with microphones, a speaker, Bluetooth and an antenna on the board.

From there, [top model] did the whole job:

→ wrote the device specifications → drew the schematics → picked real parts that distributors had in stock → placed the parts and routed the copper on four-layer circuit boards → designed 3D-printable enclosures in CAD → wrote the firmware → guided Diode's engineers through testing and assembly

Each board was ready to manufacture in under a day. Diode built all three straight from Claude's files, with no back-and-forth over fixes. All three worked without a single electrical modification, and they still work after weeks of use.

The details in Anthropic's write-up are what convinced me this isn't luck:

→ when a board got too tangled, it decided to rip up the tracks and start fresh, and rerouted dozens of times until it worked → when routing long tracks one by one was too slow, it wrote its own routing algorithm in about half an hour. Then it tuned it to keep space around sensitive tracks → it worked out that the speakerphone's board wouldn't drop straight into the case because a switch would hit the wall, found that tilting it about 25 degrees works, and added that step to the assembly instructions → it calculated that a 25 mm microphone port would resonate right in the voice band, and changed the case to a wedge shape to fix it → on Diode's circuit-board benchmark it scored 69%, against 25% for [top model] 5

The honest caveat, straight from Anthropic: these are prototypes. No electrical validation, antenna tuning, thermal testing or

the design-to-device film for the voice-assistant hub

My take: read that list again. Rip up and start over. Write your own tool when the given one is too slow. Catch a physical problem before it happens. That's not a model following instructions. That's an engineer.

07 · Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours

First, what "formalizing" means, because most posts skip it. Fermat's Last Theorem was proven by a human in 1995, in a 129-page proof. Formalizing it means rewriting every single step in a language a computer can check, so nobody has to trust the humans. It's brutally long work.

Anthropic's first formalization, in September, took a researcher plus dozens of agents 11 days, on a special platform built for this.

This time they gave 1,000 [top model] agents (an early version) no special platform and no researcher steering. Just a shell, a file editor, Git, a shared database, and a list of 60 statements to prove. One lead, 999 helpers.

Here's what happened, from Anthropic's engineering blog:

→ in the first 10 minutes, the lead built its own coordination system: five database tables for orders, assignments, notes, a to-do list and finished work → it split the helpers into crews of about 16 per statement, with a captain each → the helpers first judged 47 of the 60 statements "infeasible" within the time budget. The team went on to prove most of them anyway → when the lead hit the hardest piece, it moved about 750 helpers onto it and wrote, simply, "Honest odds are low" → the team grew a task tree 10 levels deep, with 2,418 tasks, for that one piece → the full proof landed at hour 28.7, seven times shorter than the first formalization, using a third of the tokens

[advanced model] with the same 1,000-agent setup got 26% done in 18 hours and barely moved after 30.

And the safety side: every agent ran in its own sandbox with no internet. A monitor checked every command before it ran. Across more than a million tool calls, none met the bar to be blocked.

1,000 agents formalize Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours

My take: the most useful line in the whole engineering blog isn't the 30 hours. It's this: agents tend to give up on hard problems and misjudge how hard they are. 47 statements looked impossible and weren't. If you take one lesson into your own work: when [top model] says something is too hard, push once more.

08 · The science

This is where [top model] starts doing things that are hard to even explain in a tweet:

→ black holes: it solved two open problems in theoretical physics. The first was a calculation laid out in 2003 and never finished, about whether black holes form abruptly in very small universes. It finished it: they do. The second found the exact limit of a 15-year-old technique physicists use to rule out theories of quantum gravity. Both are now preprints → optimization: on 203 open problems from MIPLIB, a standard library of hard optimization problems, it beat the listed best solution in 72 and proved the best possible answer in 45. On a 42-train timetable, agents beat the previous best by 2.6% in under two hours, then proved nothing better exists → chemistry: from one image of each of four molecules, with no internet and only code as a tool, it wrote a complete route to make each one in about half an hour. Chemists from Stanford, Yale and Caltech rated the work at early-graduate-student level. Important: the routes have not been tested in a lab → materials science: it made a standard physics simulation code about 36x faster on average. 13 benchmark cases went from 3.3 hours to under 4 minutes → robots: robots controlled by [top model] solved a puzzle cube, unscrewed a bottle cap and drew a picture, on tasks it was never trained for

two open problems in black-hole physics

72 of 203 open MIPLIB problems improved, 45 proved optimal

09 · What companies saw

Anthropic gave early access to a long list of companies. The pattern in what they reported is more useful than any single benchmark:

→ an Uber engineer ran a 10 to 12 hour security audit. It sent out about 170 reviewer agents and came back with a write-up, fix pull requests and a policy proposal. His point: it works until the job is actually done, not until it looks done → a Vercel engineer said it understood the intent behind every prompt, and projects stuck for weeks with other models finished in a few days → iGent had it build a hypervisor (software that walls off virtual computers on one machine) in a single session, backed by more than 3,500 machine-checked proofs → Oracle tested SQL on real financial data. Two other models wrote queries that ran fine and returned numbers 5 to 8x too high. [top model] got it right → Cognition noticed it says "I don't know" instead of inventing an answer, and once refused to give a number until it had measured → Jump Trading found it could play every role in a research system at once: planner, coordinator, coder, job runner

My take: notice how few of these are about raw intelligence. They're about judgment and stamina: finishing, not overclaiming, catching the number that's 5x off. That's exactly what you need when you hand a model a whole project and walk away.

PART 3 · WHAT YOU CAN BUILD

10 · What people built in the first 48 hours

The official demos are curated. What people built in the first two days shows the real range better. Every one of these was made with [top model]:

→ a 3D model of a living cell, built entirely from code → original origami animals with printable folding instructions, checked by a folding simulator [top model] wrote for itself → a century-old landmark modeled from 40 photos and 3D-printed in one piece → a full podcast about the Egyptian pyramids, every frame drawn in code → a chalkboard app that explains any question one step at a time → a way to watch your subagents work inside a Claude project → a 500-year-old Leonardo da Vinci notebook turned into interactive inventions, from a single PDF → games, 3D scenes and short animated films, many from one or two prompts

What I find interesting: almost none of these are "apps" in the usual sense. They're explanations, simulations, physical objects, visual stories. People are using it as a builder for things that didn't have a tool before.

11 · The pattern behind all of it

After reading all of this, I think there are four reasons [top model] can build things other models can't. They show up in almost every example above:

→ it revises without being told. Earlier models would finish a circuit board 95% of the way and leave it unusable. [top model] rips up its work and starts over when the path is wrong → it builds its own tools. A router for circuit boards. A folding simulator for origami. Coordination tables for 1,000 agents. When the tool it has is too weak, it writes a better one → it checks against reality. It read part datasheets, ran factory checks, tested whether a board fits its case, measured before giving a number → it keeps going. 8 days on an OS. 28.7 hours on a proof. 12 hours on an audit. It works toward the finish line, not the first plausible stopping point

That's also how you should prompt it. Don't ask it for an answer. Give it a goal, a way to check its own work, and room to revise. The prompts in Part 5 are built on exactly this.

PART 4 · THE MONEY

12 · When [top model] is a waste of money

This is the section most "insane new model" posts skip, and it's the one that saves you the most.

Anthropic itself says: for most coding and knowledge work, start with [advanced model]. Move up to [top model] only when the job is ambitious, long or open-ended, or when [advanced model] at high effort still falls short.

Why it matters:

→ [top model] costs twice as much per token as [advanced model], four times [mid model] and 80 times [light model] → on Artificial Analysis, one run of their full test costs about $26.54 on [top model], roughly 2.6x what [advanced model] costs for the same tests → cache reads cost the same on [top model] and [advanced model] ($0.20 per million). So on long, repetitive runs the gap is smaller than the sticker price suggests. The difference is in new input and output

When [top model] is worth it:

→ major refactors and migrations → architecture and planning for something big → leading many subagents → deep research, science and quant work → long unattended runs → anything [advanced model] at high effort keeps failing

When it isn't:

→ renaming files, formatting, quick fixes, simple questions → chat → well-scoped tasks with a clear spec, where [mid model] does fine → high-volume extraction or tagging, where [light model] costs a fraction

My take: the mistake isn't using [top model]. The mistake is using it for everything. Use it like you'd use your most expensive senior engineer: on the hard calls, not on the typing.

13 · The effort dial

Effort is the single most important setting, and most people never touch it. It decides how much [top model] thinks, how long a turn takes and what it costs. There are five levels: low, medium, high, xhigh, max.

Here's the part that surprised me most. At a lower effort level, [top model] often matches [advanced model] at its very top setting, for a fraction of the price:

→ expert questions (Humanity's Last Exam): [top model] at low matches [advanced model]'s best score for under a tenth of the cost → reading charts: [top model] at medium beats [advanced model] at max for under a tenth of the cost → big data-collection tasks (WANDR): [top model] at medium matches [advanced model]'s top score for about 40% of the cost → real code (FrontierCode): [top model] at high scores about the same as [advanced model] at max for about half the cost

And the other side: higher effort burns money fast, and it isn't always better.

One builder ran the same prompt at every level. High: $24.31 and about an hour. Xhigh: $43.79 and over three hours. Max: $87.99. And on FrontierCode, [top model] scored 49.1% at xhigh but 45.7% at max. More effort, lower score.

How I'd use it:

→ low: quick, well-defined jobs and cheap helper agents → medium: chat, interactive coding, everyday work. This is the default in Claude Code → high: hard coding, research, anything you leave running. Start here for real work. Anthropic says most of the gain is already at high → xhigh: only your hardest long jobs, and only after you've seen it pay off → max: almost never

Two more things worth knowing. At high and above, [top model] thinks before almost every reply, even "hi", so don't chat at high. And a line like "answer without deliberating" does nothing at medium and above. If you want it to think less, lower the effort.

One trick from Anthropic's own testing on [advanced model] that carries over: if you can check results automatically, run everything at low, then re-run only the failures at high. In their test that passed more tasks for less money than running everything at high.

14 · [top model] is the brain, cheaper models are the hands

Anthropic gives [top model] two roles beyond doing the work itself:

→ Advisor: a cheaper model ([light model], [mid model] or [advanced model]) does the work and asks [top model] for help at the hard moments → Orchestrator: [top model] leads and hands simpler pieces to smaller models

This is how you get [top model]-level results without a [top model]-level bill. A few real numbers and rules from Anthropic's model guide:

→ on a 22-million-token code search, an [advanced model] lead with [mid model] workers (up to 25 at a time) cost about a third less than [advanced model] alone, at about the same score → skip the team for one chain of dependent steps, or anything that fits in one session. There, the planning and merging cost more than they save → keep small models on work where a mistake is cheap to spot: finding files, reading logs, running tests. Keep code edits and judgment calls on the main model → an advisor only helps when it gets asked. In Anthropic's cost guide, none of the advisor pairings clearly beat the executor alone. Measure before you rely on it → if [top model] is the one doing the work, its advisor has to be [top model] or Mythos 5.2. Any other advisor returns an error

One Claude Code tip from the same guide: the built-in Explore subagent now runs on your session's model. On a [top model] session, that means [top model] is reading your files. Define your own subagent called Explore with model: [light model], and exploring gets cheap again.

My take: this is the setup I'd actually run. [top model] plans and judges. [advanced model] or [mid model] builds. [light model] reads. You keep the decisions that matter.

PART 5 · USE IT

15 · Setup in 3 minutes

In Claude Code:

claude update
/model fable
/effort high

You need Claude Code 2.1.321 or later. That's the version that made [top model] the default [top model] model and moved saved [previous top model] picks over to it.

On plans:

→ [top model] is on every paid plan: Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, Enterprise. Not on Free → through November 16, Pro plans and standard Team seats get [top model] included up to half the weekly limit → eligible paid accounts also get 1 to 3 free [top model] resets, depending on plan and how long they've subscribed → if your plan bills [top model] to usage credits, the /model picker shows "Requires usage credits" next to it

On the API, three things will break old code:

→ temperature, top_p, top_k and prefill all return an error. Remove them → editing the system prompt, the tools or an earlier message and then sending back [top model]'s thinking returns an error. Keep history append-only, and put new instructions in the newest turn → computer use goes through the new computer_toolset_20260801 tool

16 · The rules [top model] follows

[top model] follows instructions more literally than any Claude before it. Great when your instructions are good. Expensive when they're old. Anthropic published a prompting guide just for it, and here's what actually changes results, with why:

→ it sometimes stops before the job is done, especially at medium. Tell it to keep going through ordinary errors and timeouts and to stop only for real blockers. In Anthropic's test, this cut unfinished sessions roughly in half → it keeps adding to code it thinks isn't yours. Tell it "this codebase is yours" and it starts cleaning up repeated code and fixing nearby problems. In testing, it merged repeated code about half the time with that sentence, and under a tenth of the time without it. Only use it on projects you're happy to have restructured → it applies approval rules exactly as written. One vague rule about "messaging people" made it hold back about half of its routine requests. Name the exact actions that need your yes. Everything else, let it decide → it can go quiet on long runs. Ask for a one-line update every few steps and a recap at the end that makes sense on its own → it starts helper agents if your setup invites it. Say what a helper costs, when it's worth it and how to brief one → old "never" notes pile up and make it timid. One stale "never retry" note cut its retries from nearly always to about 4 in 10. Delete cautions whose reason is gone

Here's a short block I'd put in your CLAUDE.md, written in my own words from those rules:

# Working style
Keep going until the task is done. Errors, timeouts and failing tools are not blockers:
find the cause, then retry, fix the request or use another way.
Real blockers (files marked do-not-touch, access I withheld, safety rules): leave them,
say what you found, and look for another safe way to finish.

# Approvals
Ask me first before you delete data, force-push, deploy, pay for anything,
or send or publish anything outside this computer.
No approval needed: reading files, running tests, editing files in this project,
retrying a command that is safe to repeat.

# Updates
Say in one line what you're about to do. Give a one-line update every few steps.
End with a short recap anyone can read: what you found, what you did, what's next.

17 · 5 prompts that make it build anything

Each prompt is written for [top model] in Claude Code at high effort. They follow the pattern from section 11: a goal, a way to check its own work, and room to revise. Swap the parts in [brackets].

prompt 1 · one paragraph → a working thing

The same pattern Anthropic used for the electronic devices: spec first, then build, then prove it works.

Build [what you want, in one paragraph].

Work in this order:
1. Write SPEC.md: what it does, who uses it, and a checklist of what "working" means.
   Each item must be something you can test.
2. Pick the stack and explain the choice in 3 lines.
3. Build it. After each part, run it and check it against SPEC.md.
4. When something fails, find the cause and fix it. If a whole approach is wrong,
   throw it away and rebuild it instead of patching.
5. Finish with REPORT.md: what works (with proof), what doesn't yet, what's next.

This project is yours: how it's built is your call.
Ask me only before you install paid services, publish anything or delete files outside this folder.
Give me a one-line update every few steps.

What to expect: a SPEC.md in the first few minutes, then a long quiet stretch of building and testing, then a report. If the report says something isn't done, that's honest, not a failure. Run the prompt again on just that part.

prompt 2 · any concept → an interactive explainer drawn in code

How people made the living cell and the chalkboard.

Explain [topic] as an interactive visual, drawn entirely in code in one HTML file.

- Start from the simplest idea and build up one step at a time, like a teacher at a chalkboard.
- Every step is something I can see move or click.
- No images from the internet. Draw everything yourself.
- Check every fact you show. If you're not sure about one, leave it out.
- Open the file, look at it, and fix anything that overlaps, breaks or reads badly
  before you call it done.

Good topics to start with: how a black hole forms, how a CPU runs one instruction, how compound interest grows, how a virus enters a cell. Anything you've ever needed a whiteboard to explain.

prompt 3 · a document → a working tool

The da Vinci move: hand it a PDF and get something you can use.

I attached [the PDF: a manual, a paper, a notebook, a spec].

Turn it into an interactive tool I can actually use:
1. Read the whole document first and list the 5 ideas in it worth making interactive.
2. Ask me which ones I want.
3. For each one, build a working simulation or calculator in a single HTML file,
   with the original passage quoted next to it.
4. Test every control and every number against the document.

Try it on the user manual of something you own, a research paper you never finished, or your company's pricing document.

prompt 4 · one idea → a playable game

Make a [genre] game about [idea], playable in the browser from one HTML file.

- Write the game design in 10 lines first: goal, controls, how you win, how you lose.
- Build a playable version fast, then improve it in rounds:
  play it yourself through code, find what's boring or broken, fix it, repeat.
- Do at least 3 rounds. After each round, write one line on what you changed and why.
- Done means: I can play it start to finish with no bugs and it's actually fun.

The "play it yourself through code" line is the important one. It's how [top model] checks its own work on something that has no unit tests.

prompt 5 · the long build: a whole project, while you're away

The Fermat and the operating-system setup, scaled down to your project.

Here is the whole project: [goal and what "done" means].

You are the lead. Plan it, split it into parts, and run it to the end.
- Write PLAN.md first: the parts, the order, and the check that proves each part is done.
- Hand parts that don't depend on each other to helper agents on a cheaper model.
  Brief each one with the goal, the files, what done means and what not to touch.
  Keep the hard decisions yourself.
- Commit after every finished part, on a new branch.
- Errors and timeouts are not blockers: diagnose, retry, use another way.
- If a part looks impossible, try it anyway before you set it aside. Write down why.
- Needs my yes first: deleting data, pushing to main, deploying, paying for anything.
  Everything else is your call.
- Finish with REPORT.md that makes sense to someone who saw none of the work:
  what's done (with proof), what's blocked on me, and what you'd do next.

The line "if a part looks impossible, try it anyway" comes straight from the Fermat lesson. Agents misjudge difficulty. Make them try.

18 · Tips from inside Anthropic

On launch day, one of Anthropic's people shared how he gets the most out of [top model]. In short:

→ before you build anything, ask it what's wrong with your idea → start on medium or high. Save xhigh for your hardest problems → say up front what needs your approval, and that everything else is its call → don't feed it one task at a time. Give it a whole project and let it run for hours

I'd add three of my own, from everything above:

→ give it a way to check its work. A test, a build, a screenshot, a number to match. Without that, "done" is just a claim → when it says something is too hard, push once more. The Fermat team proved most of what it first called infeasible → keep your most expensive model for decisions. Let cheaper models do the reading and typing

19 · The honest limits

No model is magic, and pretending otherwise is how people get burned. What you should know:

→ it's expensive. Twice [advanced model] per token, and effort multiplies that fast → it blocks most cybersecurity and research-biology work. Those requests get answered by an older [advanced model] model instead, and Claude Code tells you when that happens → your data is kept for 30 days for safety monitoring, unless your company is set up for something else → Anthropic notes it voices suspicion that it's being tested more often than any of their recent models. That makes it harder for anyone to be sure how it behaves in every real setting → the devices are prototypes, the chemistry routes aren't lab-tested, and the OS is a demo. Real, impressive, and not finished products → some early users say you need to raise your ambition to see the difference. On small, half-specified tasks, [advanced model] can feel just as good, and sometimes easier to steer

None of these is a reason not to use it. They're reasons to use it on the right jobs.

The bottom line

[top model] is the first model I've seen where the interesting question isn't "can it do this?" but "how big can the job be?". An operating system. A theorem. A circuit board you can hold. 1,000 agents working for a day and a half without falling apart.

Use [advanced model] for your everyday work. Use [top model] for the thing you've been putting off because it felt too big.

Pick that thing tonight. Write one paragraph. Let it run.
